title: Japan Pilgrimage
speaker: Seiu Hannah Sullivan, Joden Bob Rose and Seishu John Wiley
summary: The speaker reflects on their experiences visiting various temples and shrines in Japan, including traditional Zen monasteries and cultural sites, which deepened their understanding of Soto Zen principles. They share stories about the warmth and hospitality they encountered at each site, as well as the unique architecture, art, and culture they observed. Through these experiences, the speaker came to appreciate the importance of mindfulness, community, and connection with nature in Zen practice, and how these values can be found in everyday life.

This is our hotel, Matsubaya Ryokan, where we began and ended our trip in Kyoto.
It's a typical Japanese inn for travelers.
You get a Japanese breakfast or an American, a Western breakfast.
Most of the rooms have a futon: you sleep on it and then you fold it up and put it away, because they're very small rooms compared to what we're used to in U.S. hotels.
They're very comfortable.
This is two blocks from the major Pure Land temple in Japan and half a mile from the train station.
Our tour guides were Michael Newton and Kate McCandless.
This is inside the rooms, small.
You take your shoes off very, very religiously when you get into the hotel.
You go in with a pair of shoes on to walk the stairs from the hallway, walk into your room, onto a wooden floor, take the shoes off, put on slippers, and then step up onto this tatami mat floor.
Rooms are measured in how many tatami mats it would take to fill the room.
We have one right here.
You can see it under the altar here.
And they're incredibly comfortable, these futons.
They have a really cool way of making the puff that you get fitted with a little sheet, so you've got a whole deal that you're just snuggled up in, in your bed.
This is Kenninji, the first Zen monastery in Kyoto.
Our first day we visited here.
After that we visited Mount Hiei, which I think is the next slide.
These are both places that Dogen was.
This is the entrance to Mount Hiei, which was the first temple complex built in the Kyoto area.
Actually, it was before Kyoto even became the capital city, while Nara was still the capital of Japan.
Dogen studied here, and also Saicho, who is the founder of the Shingon sect of Buddhism, and Kobo Daishi, whose monastery area, Mount Koya, we visited, also studied here.
This is the major Buddhist temple in Japan in the 7th through the 12th century.
Dogen studied here as a boy, and then left, because he felt that he needed to find more.
It's also on the northwest edge of the mountain, so it was built there as a guard against evil spirits, according to Chinese tradition.
That was the main temple there, the first main temple on Mount Hiei.
This painting was on the ceiling of a temple.
It's as big as a basketball court.
I think it was done in about 2003 to commemorate the 200th anniversary or something like that of the temple.
It took the artist two years to do it.
It's incredible.
I believe the ceiling size is 108 tatami mats.
He set this up in a grade school gymnasium and covered the floor with this thick rice paper.
I watched a film of how he did it.
You see how this looks like it's been airbrushed?

He would sit with his knees on some kind of pad so he wouldn't mess up the painting, and then take a brush that was probably 12, 16 inches wide and just wield it around the edges of anything [unclear: "if you wanted to blow it"].
So water dragging the painting on the ceiling to protect the temple from fire, because that was such a great danger.
Stunning.
This is sort of the Sesame Street slideshow crew here.

You can kind of see here, it's like we've got two slides overlaid, but this is one of the screens of that same temple.

This is Fushimi Inari, the red torii gate shrine south of Kyoto.

The saying in Japan is that Japanese people are born Shinto and die Buddhist.
Shinto was a religion that was there before Buddhism came to Japan in the fifth or sixth century.
It's a religion of kind of earth fertility, and the image you often see is a fox with a sheaf of rice in his mouth at these various shrines.
This is one of the entry shrines there.
There are 7,000 of those gates wandering up the mountain.
The red is always indicative of Shinto, and these little zigzaggy pieces, you find trees that have been circled with them, and anything that wants to be blessed.
Beautiful, beautiful.
This is the entry gate to Rinso-in, Suzuki Roshi's home monastery, where we spent four days with the family, and there will be some pictures that follow from us.
So we were their guests.
It's a beautiful temple, it's in really good shape.
It's clean and well maintained, with beautiful gardens.
There are creeks running on both sides, so you can always hear running water.
It's really a pretty place.
And it's just built right into this deep mountainside.
It's actually built between [unclear: "our two channelized now creeks come down and it's five feet deep"].

Every day they would come and say hello.

This is inside the zendō.
I took this picture because I sat in that kind of far right corner.

I believe maybe 12 monks lived there.
So these are six of the boxes of each monk.

Yeah, that's yet to come.

And lo and behold, she's a teacher of that.
She gave us an afternoon of her time where she taught us all kinds of things about how she arranges flowers.
She took me through the temple.
She had me change out all the vases and showed us how to bring the flowers toward the person who would be looking at them.
You have to face the flower.
That's right.
So you'll be the flower she met, our next teacher.
She was amazing.
Amazingly spry for her age, too.
Quite a Dharma teacher.
Yeah, no kidding.
Tiny little woman.

Frog.

Here's a remarkable demonstration of a particular kind of Soto chanting, bells and cymbals with notation for notes.
Instead of notating music on a staff with a vertical kind of framework, as we do, this nomenclature is using a compass.
Straight up is C and then northeast is D and it kind of goes around that way.
So the notation is kind of a compass, and then the length of the line is the length the note is held, and then it would be a triangle or a circle for where a bell or a chime was rung.
It was quite extraordinary.
And then he just performed it for us.
It was beautiful.
And just dynamic, really.
It's like a martial arts teacher.
Yeah, so much.
And again, funny.
They really were.
And I have to say that my takeaway memory from the Dharma talks is that after Hojo-sama gave us this pretty intense Dharma talk about what it was like to be Suzuki Roshi's son.
It wasn't easy.

Practice with joy.
Not because you think you have to or because you've got something you've got to work out.
Just practice with joy."

The whole family was extraordinarily kind and warm and welcoming, even the little kids.

These people just were so warm and kind.
It was just incredible.
This is Shango's wife and your daughter.

I'm going to take you into town," and bundled up everybody into the car.

And these are great symbols of what it takes.
